lessons.title: How Leverage Magnifies Both Engines and Both Losses

children.text: "Why pay ₹1 crore cash when you can put down ₹25 lakh and let the bank fund the rest? If prices rise 10%, you make ₹10 lakh on a ₹25 lakh investment. That is 40%!" Every property investor in India hears some version of this pitch. The arithmetic is not wrong, but it is incomplete. The same loan that turns a 10% rise into a large gain turns a 10% fall into a disaster, and it charges interest every month whether prices move or not. By the end of this lesson you will be able to calculate your return on equity with a loan, find the appreciation you need just to break even on the interest, and stress-test a leveraged purchase before you sign.

body.text: A home loan does not change what a property earns. It changes who gets the result. If the property's total return beats your loan rate, leverage multiplies your gain. If it does not, leverage multiplies your loss, and flat prices become a loss.

children.text: How Leverage Works

markDefs.definition: Using borrowed money to buy an asset, so that gains and losses on the full asset value fall on your smaller own investment.
Loan-to-value ratio: the loan amount as a percentage of the property's value. A ₹75 lakh loan on a ₹1 crore flat is a 75% LTV.
The annual gain or loss on the money you personally put in, after interest, expressed as a percentage of that money.

children.text: Leverage
means the property's rent and appreciation are earned on its full value, while you have only put in part of that value yourself. The share funded by the bank is the
LTV
. What matters to you is the
return on equity
: what you gain or lose on your own money after paying interest.

Take a ₹1 crore flat earning a 2.5% net yield (₹2.5 lakh a year). One buyer pays cash. Another puts down ₹25 lakh and borrows ₹75 lakh at 8.5%. For a clean one-year comparison, treat interest as 8.5% of the loan, about ₹6.4 lakh, and ignore buying costs and tax.

body.caption: One year on a ₹1 crore flat: cash buyer vs 75% loan (illustrative)
R = the property's unlevered total return (net yield + appreciation), i = loan interest rate, D ÷ E = loan divided by your own money. At 75% LTV, D ÷ E = 3.

children.text: Check it for the +10% year: R = 12.5%, i = 8.5%, so ROE = 12.5% + (12.5% − 8.5%) × 3 = 24.5%. For the −10% year: R = −7.5%, so ROE = −7.5% + (−7.5% − 8.5%) × 3 = −55.5%. The loan triples the gap between the property's return and the interest rate, in whichever direction that gap points.

body.title: One-Year Return on Your Own Money by Loan Size (%)
body.xAxisLabel: Property price change in the year

body.text: Look at the 0% column. With no loan, a year of flat prices still earns the 2.5% rent. With a 75% loan, the same year loses 15.5% of your own money, because interest runs at 8.5% while the property earns only 2.5%. And at +5%, the loan buyer does worse than the cash buyer. Leverage is not a bet that prices will rise. It is a bet that they will rise faster than your loan costs.

body.title: Calculate return on equity
body.prompt: A ₹60 lakh flat in Vadodara is bought with a 75% loan at 9%. In the first year, its price rises 8% and it earns a 3% net yield. Using ROE = R + (R − i) × D ÷ E, and ignoring costs and tax, what is the return on the buyer's own money?
body.explanation: R = 8% + 3% = 11%. D ÷ E = 75 ÷ 25 = 3. ROE = 11% + (11% − 9%) × 3 = 17%. In rupees: gain = ₹4.8 lakh appreciation + ₹1.8 lakh rent − ₹4.05 lakh interest = ₹2.55 lakh on ₹15 lakh of own money, which is 17%.

children.text: When Leverage Helps and When It Hurts

markDefs.definition: When an asset's total return is higher than the interest rate on the money borrowed to buy it, so borrowing increases your return.
When an asset's total return is lower than the borrowing rate, so borrowing reduces your return or deepens your loss.

children.text: The formula gives you the one test that matters. If R is above i, you have
positive leverage
. If R is below i, you have
negative leverage
. Because Indian residential yields are so low, almost all of R has to come from appreciation.

body.caption: Before buying costs and tax. For the ₹1 crore flat: 8.5% − 2.5% = 6% a year, just to make the loan worth having.

columns.label: Positive leverage (total return above loan rate)
points: Each borrowed rupee earns more than it costs
Return on equity is higher than the cash buyer's return
More likely with higher-yield commercial property or falling interest rates
Needs appreciation above about 6% a year on a 2.5% yield flat at 8.5%

columns.label: Negative leverage (total return below loan rate)
points: Each borrowed rupee costs more than it earns
Return on equity is lower than the cash buyer's, and often negative
Common with low-yield flats when prices grow slowly
Flat or falling prices turn into large losses on your own money

body.title: Does the loan help?
body.question: A flat earns a 2.5% net yield and appreciates 5% a year. The owner's home loan costs 8.5%. Ignoring costs and tax, what is the effect of using a 75% loan instead of paying cash?
options: It raises the return on equity, because prices are rising
It lowers the return on equity, because the total return of 7.5% is below the 8.5% loan rate
It has no effect, because the property earns the same either way
It doubles the return on equity
body.explanation: R = 7.5%, i = 8.5%. ROE = 7.5% + (7.5% − 8.5%) × 3 = 4.5%, below the cash buyer's 7.5%. Rising prices alone are not enough; they must rise fast enough that yield plus appreciation beats the loan rate.

children.text: Ten Years With Real EMIs: The XIRR View

One-year arithmetic hides the monthly reality of EMIs. Here is the same ₹1 crore flat over ten years using the XIRR method from the last lesson. Both buyers pay ₹7 lakh in buying costs in cash. Net rent starts at ₹2.5 lakh and grows 5% a year. The loan buyer pays an EMI of about ₹65,100 a month on ₹75 lakh at 8.5% over 20 years, about ₹7.81 lakh a year, and still owes about ₹52.5 lakh when the flat is sold after ten years with 1% brokerage. Returns are before tax.

body.caption: Ten-year XIRR on own money: cash vs 75% loan (illustrative, before tax)

children.text: This is the most sobering table in the course. Even with a strong 7% a year of appreciation, the loan barely improves the return, because after buying costs the property earns only about 8.4% a year, almost exactly the 8.5% loan rate. At 3% growth, the loan wipes out nearly all of the return. At 0%, it turns a small positive return into a heavy loss. Meanwhile, the loan buyer must fund a gap of about ₹5.3 lakh from salary in the very first year.
Interest Rate Risk: The Engine You Do Not Control

markDefs.definition: External benchmark lending rate: since October 2019, new floating-rate home loans from banks are linked to an external benchmark, most commonly RBI's repo rate, so changes pass through to borrowers faster.

children.text: Most Indian home loans are floating-rate, and bank loans are typically linked to an
external benchmark

such as RBI's repo rate. Between May 2022 and February 2023, RBI raised the repo rate from 4% to 6.5%, and home loan rates rose by a similar amount. When rates rise, lenders usually extend your loan tenure first to keep the EMI unchanged, which can quietly add years of payments.

body.title: Show me the math: how a rate rise stretches the tenure

children.text: A ₹75 lakh loan at 7% for 20 years has an EMI of about ₹58,100. After two years of payments, about ₹71.3 lakh is still owed. If the rate rises to 9.5%, monthly interest on that balance is about ₹56,400, so the unchanged EMI repays only about ₹1,700 of principal a month at first. Solving for the months needed gives about 448 more months, or roughly 39 years in total instead of 20.

content.caption: n = remaining months, B = outstanding balance, r = new monthly rate. If EMI is not larger than B × r, the loan would never be repaid.

children.text: In practice, lenders cap tenure by the borrower's age, so a rise this large usually means a higher EMI as well. Borrowers can also choose to pay a higher EMI or prepay to limit the extension. Always ask your lender which option has been applied after a rate change.
The Worst Case: Negative Equity

markDefs.definition: When a property is worth less than the loan outstanding on it, so selling would not even repay the bank.

children.text: The higher the LTV, the smaller the price fall needed to wipe out your equity entirely. A ₹30 lakh flat bought with a 90% loan of ₹27 lakh needs to fall only 10% to erase the ₹3 lakh down payment. At a 15% fall, the flat is worth ₹25.5 lakh against a ₹27 lakh loan:
negative equity
. If you lose your job or need to relocate, selling would leave you owing the bank money with no flat, after having already paid buying costs and years of EMIs.

body.caption: RBI's maximum loan-to-value limits for housing loans

cells: Above ₹30 lakh and up to ₹75 lakh

body.text: Be wary of any scheme that promises to fund more than these limits, such as "pay only 5% now" offers that combine a home loan with a developer's deferred payment or a personal loan for the down payment. Extra borrowing at higher rates pushes your true leverage far above the RBI cap and makes negative equity much more likely.

body.title: Name the ratio
body.textWithBlank: A ₹90 lakh home loan on a ₹1.2 crore flat represents a 75% ___ ratio.
body.explanation: Loan-to-value (LTV) = loan ÷ property value = ₹90 lakh ÷ ₹1.2 crore = 75%, which is RBI's maximum for loans above ₹75 lakh.

body.title: Stress-test an investment flat
body.scenario: Vivek Nair, a 32-year-old product manager in Bengaluru with a take-home salary of ₹1.8 lakh a month, wants to buy a second flat as an investment on Thanisandra Main Road for ₹1.2 crore. A broker says: "You can get an 80% loan, so just ₹24 lakh down. Rent of ₹25,000 will cover a big part of the EMI, and prices here will rise 8% a year." Buying costs are about 7% (₹8.4 lakh). Home loan rates are 8.5% for 20 years. Net rent after costs is about ₹25,000 a month, a 2.5% net yield.
body.prompt: Check the broker's claims against RBI's LTV limits, calculate the monthly gap, find the break-even appreciation, and stress-test the plan for a 2 percentage point rate rise and a year of flat prices.
body.modelAnswer:
1. LTV: a loan above ₹75 lakh is capped at 75%, so the maximum is ₹90 lakh, not ₹96 lakh. Vivek needs ₹30 lakh down plus ₹8.4 lakh in buying costs: ₹38.4 lakh of own money.
2. Monthly gap: the EMI on ₹90 lakh at 8.5% for 20 years is about ₹78,100. Rent of ₹25,000 covers under a third. The gap is about ₹53,100 a month, roughly 30% of take-home pay, on top of Vivek's own living costs and any existing home loan.
3. Break-even appreciation: 8.5% − 2.5% = about 6% a year before costs and tax, just for the loan to add anything. The broker's 8% would give positive leverage, but only if it actually happens year after year.
4. Rate shock: at 10.5%, the EMI on ₹90 lakh rises to about ₹89,900 (or the tenure stretches). The gap grows to about ₹64,900 a month, about 36% of take-home pay.
5. A flat year: using the one-year approximation, R = 2.5% and i = 8.5% at 75% LTV gives ROE = 2.5% + (2.5% − 8.5%) × 3 = −15.5% on the ₹30 lakh equity, a loss of roughly ₹4.65 lakh, before counting buying costs already sunk.
6. Further checks: can Vivek fund the gap for a year if the flat is vacant or if salary stops? Is there an emergency fund of at least six months of total EMIs? What is the actual resale price trend on that road, not the broker's forecast? And how would the numbers look with a smaller loan or a lower-priced flat?

body.title: Stress-test any leveraged property purchase
steps: Confirm the maximum loan under RBI's LTV limits and include buying costs in your own contribution.
Calculate the monthly gap between EMI and net rent, and express it as a share of take-home pay.
Find the break-even appreciation: loan rate minus net yield.
Recalculate the EMI, or the extended tenure, at a rate 2 percentage points higher.
Estimate the loss on your own money in a year of flat or falling prices.
Check how far prices could fall before you reach negative equity.
Make sure an emergency fund can cover at least six months of EMIs with no rent and no salary.

cards.definition: Using borrowed money so gains and losses on the full asset fall on your smaller own investment.
Loan-to-value: loan amount as a percentage of property value. RBI caps it at 90%, 80% or 75% depending on loan size.
ROE = R + (R − i) × D ÷ E, the return on your own money after interest.
Total return above the loan rate, so borrowing raises your return.
Total return below the loan rate, so borrowing lowers your return or deepens losses.
Roughly the loan rate minus net rental yield: the growth needed for a loan to add value.
When a property is worth less than the loan outstanding on it.

points: Leverage does not change what a property earns; it concentrates the result on your smaller own investment.
Return on equity = R + (R − i) × D ÷ E. At 75% LTV, the loan triples the gap between total return and the loan rate.
With a 2.5% net yield and an 8.5% loan, prices must rise about 6% a year before the loan adds anything.
In a year of flat prices, a 75% loan turns a 2.5% return into roughly a 15.5% loss on your own money.
Over ten years, even 7% annual appreciation barely made the loan worthwhile once buying costs were included.
Floating rates can rise sharply, raising EMIs or stretching tenures by many years.
High LTVs bring negative equity close; respect RBI's LTV limits and avoid stacking extra loans on top.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, lending or tax advice. The people, properties, rents, rates and growth scenarios shown are illustrative, and returns are calculated before tax. Loan terms, LTV rules and interest rates change, so confirm current terms with your lender and consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before borrowing to buy property.
